title: Sakana AI ships Fugu Max and Fugu Ultra v2 as learned multi-agent orchestrators
subtitle: Tokyo lab's newest release replaces the single-model frontier with a router that dispatches queries to a curated pool of open-weight and specialist models.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Sakana AI released Fugu Max and Fugu Ultra v2 on September 11, 2026. Both models share one architecture — a language model trained to route incoming tasks across a fixed pool of open and specialist models, and to recursively call instances of itself when a task demands it. They ship with a single OpenAI-compatible API, configurable reasoning effort levels of high, xhigh, and max, function calling, structured outputs, image and PDF input, and built-in web search. Fugu Ultra v2 is priced at five dollars per million input tokens and thirty dollars per million output tokens, with a fifty-cent cached-input rate.

The mechanism is what makes this release worth attention. Instead of one monolithic model absorbing every workload, Fugu learns which underlying model — or which subagent — to hand a subproblem to. Sakana says Fugu Ultra v2 does not rely on individual proprietary frontier models in its pool, which means its ceiling is set by open weights and specialists rather than by a single vendor's API. That decoupling matters for anyone tracking whether the frontier stays inside three or four labs or diffuses outward.

Multi-agent orchestration has been the industry story of the last twelve months — Anthropic's managed agents, OpenAI's Agents API public beta this week, Google's A2A protocol going to the Linux Foundation. Sakana's angle is different: rather than a runtime that hosts agents, Fugu ships as a single model whose internal behavior is orchestration. That collapses a lot of application code — routing, tool selection, subagent spawning — into pretrained weights. Whether learned orchestrators outperform hand-written pipelines is now testable at production scale.

For learners, the interesting question is not which model wins the benchmark. It is how the boundary between 'model' and 'system' keeps moving. A year ago 'call GPT-4 with a prompt' was a complete answer. Today the answer is more likely to involve routing, subagents, tool calls, and cached context. Fugu is one data point in that shift. If you are building on top of AI, spend the hour to read how it decides what to call — the shape of that decision will matter more than the leaderboard number.
